title: ALM-MTA: Front-Door Causal Multi-Touch Attribution Method for Creator-Ecosystem Optimization
one_liner: Estimate which recommendation exposures truly cause more creator activity by modeling the mediator path from exposure to consumption to later uploads, instead of trusting raw correlations in messy platform logs.
lead: Large creator platforms need to know which recommendation touches actually cause more creator activity, not merely which touches happen before an upload. Raw logs are confounded because stronger creators may get more exposure and also upload more anyway. This paper uses a front-door causal strategy. It builds a learned mediator that captures the pathway from exposure to consumption and then to creator output, so attribution depends on the causal route rather than on shortcut correlations in the logs.

problem.h2: Why recommendation logs do not equal causal credit
paras: On a social platform, a creator may upload more after getting exposure. But that does not prove the exposure caused the upload. High-quality creators are already more active, already get more exposure, and already attract more consumption. A plain correlation model gives too much credit to touches that happen around successful creators because it cannot separate true lift from pre-existing strength.

Backdoor adjustment helps only when the platform records all important confounders, because otherwise the missing factors still leak into the estimated effect. In practice many factors are missing or poorly measured. The paper uses a different route: if exposure changes consumption, and consumption then changes later production, the platform can identify causal credit through that mediator path even when direct confounding is hard to measure.

callout.html: Attribute credit through the exposure-to-consumption-to-production path, not through raw exposure-outcome correlation.

panels.title: 1. A creator gets several recommendation touches
panels.viz_args: Home feed, notifications, and other product surfaces expose the creator's content to users.
panels.caption: Many touches happen before any later upload or daily activity change.

panels.title: 2. Raw credit is misleading
panels.caption: A raw model confuses "already strong creator" with "touch caused extra output."

panels.title: 3. Measure the mediator path
panels.viz_args: Exposure changes consumption; consumption then influences later creator production.
panels.caption: The mediator captures the causal route the platform cares about.

panels.title: 4. Learn credit on matched pairs
panels.caption: Matched consumption-upload pairs and mediator learning make attribution more operational.

panels.title: 5. Platform policy gets better
panels.caption: Recommendation effort is shifted toward touches that truly lift creator output.

steps.text: Treatment is exposure, mediator is later consumption behavior, and outcome is creator activity such as uploads.
Train a model to capture the part of consumption that carries outcome information rather than shortcut correlations.
Use contrastive pairing so the front-door estimate has support in the large action space.
Estimate how much creator activity changes across treatment groups using bucketed non-personalized evaluation.
Use the estimated uplift to guide exposure allocation and creator incentives.

paras: The paper changes what receives attribution credit. Instead of crediting a touch because it appears near a later upload, it credits a touch when it changes the mediator in a way that then changes creator output. That is a tighter object because it removes much of the credit that comes from pre-existing creator strength.
object.object: the mediated causal effect of recommendation touches on creator output

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: clean mediator quality
hidden.name: how well the learned mediator carries true causal pathway information without shortcut leakage
paras: Front-door attribution depends on the mediator being informative for the real pathway from exposure to outcome. If the mediator mostly records shortcut signals tied to already successful creators, causal credit is still distorted. The hidden quantity is therefore mediator quality: does the learned representation capture the consequence of exposure on consumption in a way that genuinely explains later production?

ALM-MTA improves this quantity with adversarial learning and matched pair construction, because the mediator is pushed to preserve outcome-relevant pathway information while suppressing shortcut correlations, and the matching step ensures the estimate compares treatment cases that have real overlap.

heat.caption: Dark cells show where mediator quality determines whether attribution reflects true lift or just correlated popularity.

reads.html: The mediator should answer a practical question: did the touch actually change what users consumed in a way that then changed what the creator did?
ALM-MTA learns an adversarial mediator for front-door identification and conditions estimation on matched consumption-upload pairs so that the mediated effect is better identified.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: identify the path that carries the effect
paras: The method works because it shifts attribution onto a pathway that can still be identified when direct confounding is severe. Exposure affects user consumption, and that changed consumption can affect later creator output. If the mediator representation captures that path well, the method can estimate causal lift even when many creator-specific confounders are missing.

The matched-pair step matters because front-door estimation needs overlap. In a huge action space, some treatment levels may have almost no comparable cases. By conditioning on high-match consumption-upload pairs, the method estimates lift in regions where the comparison is credible, so the resulting policy scores are more dependable.

stages.s: Recommendation exposure logs, user consumption logs, and creator activity logs
Learn a mediator for the exposure-to-consumption path
Match comparable cases with similar consumption-upload structure
Estimate grouped uplift through the mediated path
Attribution scores that are useful for creator-ecosystem policy

math.words: Causal effect of a touch = sum over mediator states of how the touch changes the mediator times how the mediator changes the outcome
math.equation: Effect(x) = sum_m P(m | x) * sum_x' P(y | x', m) P(x')
symbols: a recommendation touch or treatment level
the mediator state that summarizes consumption change
the creator outcome, such as later uploads or active days
how the outcome behaves for a given mediator state

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a touch can move a creator into either a low-consumption mediator state or a high-consumption mediator state.
Assume the touch produces the high-consumption state 60 percent of the time and the low-consumption state 40 percent of the time.
In the high-consumption state the expected upload rate is 0.30, while in the low-consumption state it is 0.10.
The mediated expected outcome is therefore 0.6 x 0.30 + 0.4 x 0.10 = 0.22.
A competing touch with weaker effect on the mediator would receive less causal credit because it changes the pathway less.

math.note: The equation credits a touch when it changes the mediator and the mediator then changes the outcome, which is why it is less sensitive to raw popularity correlations.

bars.h2: Why mediated attribution is more useful than raw correlation

charts.title: Correlation-based attribution
charts.note: Raw correlation overcredits already successful creators because exposure and later uploads are both driven by hidden strength.

charts.title: ALM-MTA front-door attribution
charts.note: Mediated attribution improves policy value because it rewards touches that move the pathway rather than touches that merely surround strong creators.

items.b: The mediator may omit key pathway information.
items.html: If the learned mediator misses the part of consumption that truly drives later creator output, the front-door estimate can still be biased because the pathway is only partly observed.

items.b: Overlap may be weak in rare treatment regions.
items.html: Some touches or creator states may have too few comparable cases. Then even matched estimation is unstable because the method has little evidence for those parts of the action space.

items.b: Platform dynamics may violate the assumed path.
items.html: A touch might affect creator behavior through routes other than measured consumption, such as direct notifications or payment expectations. Those extra routes weaken the front-door story because not all causal flow passes through the mediator.
The method is strongest when consumption is the main bridge between exposure and later production, because then the mediator captures most of the causal effect the platform wants to optimize.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small synthetic creator platform with hidden creator strength, recommendation touches, user consumption, and later uploads. First estimate touch value with plain correlation and show that it mostly chases already strong creators. Then run a front-door estimator with a learned mediator and compare predicted uplift against the known simulated ground truth. The front-door version should rank touches more accurately because it uses the causal path rather than raw co-occurrence.

A second view should sort creators into policy buckets using each method. The better method should place more budget on creators whose uploads truly increase when exposure changes, not just on creators who were active already, because only the first group delivers real incremental lift.
demo.closing: A convincing demo should show that attribution quality is best judged by whether intervention choices improve outcomes, because correlation with past success can stay high even when the policy is causally wrong.
